Have you ever felt the pulse of a city that never sleeps?

San Nicolás is the neighborhood of contrasts: where our flag was born and where today the neon lights of the mythical Corrientes Street shine. Let's discover where the lives of Evita and Perón crossed, what secrets the domes of the Güemes Gallery hold, and why this corner of Buenos Aires was the dream of architects and visionaries. We will walk along Corrientes Avenue, among historic theaters and old bookstores; visit La Ideal Confectionery and the Güemes Gallery, the city's first skyscraper and home to Saint-Exupéry; discover the majesty of the Teatro Colón and the historic Plaza Lavalle; and we will reach, from Luna Park to the Obelisk, the stories that marked the destiny of Belgrano, Perón, and Evita.


If you wish, we will share a free mate experience while we unravel the secrets of the downtown area (request it in advance).


Important information:

Meeting point: Libertad 815 (in front of the Teatro Nacional Cervantes)

We start on time to respect your time and that of the group

Upon booking, I will send you my real-time location via WhatsApp and a complimentary PDF guide of Buenos Aires


\"San Nicolás is not visited. It is felt. Between the echo of the Obelisk and the murmur of Corrientes, the city tells you who it was... and who it still is.\"

Discover the charm of one of the most fascinating neighborhoods in Buenos Aires: Recoleta.

\"Although English is not my native language, my passion and enthusiasm for Buenos Aires have inspired me to create this tour in English. With my intermediate-advanced level of English, I hope to offer you an experience that you will truly enjoy.\" 


On this tour, I will take you to explore its most elegant corners, where history, art, and architecture come together to tell the story of a city that dreamed of becoming a cultural powerhouse in the early 20th century.

You will walk past impressive palaces, European-style mansions, and monuments that witnessed the golden age of Buenos Aires. Throughout the tour, I will reveal the secrets of the most influential families of that time, who left their mark on these majestic buildings.

We will also learn about the work of French landscaper Carlos Thays, who transformed a dry city into a green urban paradise. His vision made Buenos Aires a place full of parks and green spaces, which today bring beauty and life to its historic streets and avenues.

This tour is not just a journey into the past but a unique experience to discover the cultural and architectural evolution of the city.
Get ready to see it with new eyes!!!

Bienvenidos a Recoleta, el barrio que se viste de gala para que no noten que, debajo del mármol, hay historia, poder, olvido y una Argentina que se niega a mirarse en el espejo.

No venimos a ver mansiones. Venimos a descubrir quiénes las hicieron, quiénes las habitaron y quiénes quedaron afuera.

Este no es un paseo por palacios. Es un recorrido por las decisiones que construyeron (y deshicieron) un país.

¿Sabías que este barrio nació de una epidemia? En 1871, la fiebre amarilla diezmó el sur de la ciudad. Los ricos huyeron. Y eligieron este lugar: más alto, más ventilado, más lejos de los pobres. Así nació Recoleta, no por belleza, sino por exclusión.

Vamos a caminar por la Avenida Alvear, esa calle que parece sacada de París, con mansiones de piedra, balcones de hierro forjado y autos que cuestan más que una casa en el conurbano. Vamos a pararnos frente al Hotel Alvear, el Palacio Duhau, el Jockey Club, el Palacio Pereda, la Nunciatura Apostólica. Y vamos a preguntarnos: ¿Quiénes eran estos hombres que construyeron palacios como si fueran reyes? ¿Qué hicieron con su dinero? ¿Y qué hicieron con su poder?

¿Qué vas a ver?

Plaza de Francia

Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (con entrada)

Plaza Alvear

Iglesia del Pilar

Centro Cultural Recoleta

Cementerio de la Recoleta

Hotel Alvear

Residencia Mc Guire

Palacio Duhau

Palacio de la Nunciatura

Palacio Pereda

Jockey Club

Plaza Carlos Pellegrini

Este tour es para vos si…

No te conformás con decir “qué lindo” y querés saber por qué.

Te interesa la historia, pero no como una lista de fechas, sino como una conversación con el presente.

Querés entender Argentina no desde el asado ni el tango, sino desde sus contradicciones.

Hablás español, sí, pero también quieres escuchar lo que no se dice.

Soy Inés, docente, viajera y cronista. He caminado estos adoquines muchas veces, no como turista, sino como alguien que busca entender. Este tour no es un trabajo. Es una conversación que se renueva cada vez.

 

PUNTO DE ENCUENTRO

Av. del Libertador 1473, en las escalinatas del Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes. 

 

NO LO OLVIDES 

Zapatillas cómodas, agua, ropa ligera.

 

IMPORTANTE: EL PASEO SE SUSPENDE POR LLUVIA

From the Casa Rosada to the Congress, there is a route that sums up a large part of Argentine history: the domes and their symbols, the cafes where politics and literature were crafted, the buildings we all pass by but few truly observe. We will walk through Plaza de Mayo —from the Cabildo to the Cathedral where San Martín rests—, discover Dante's mark in the Barolo Palace, and sit with a view of the Tortoni and London City, witnesses of poets and conspiracies, until we reach the dome of the Congress to understand how this path shaped today's Argentina.


And as always, we share some mate along the way (order it free of charge up to 2 hours before the tour) to chat about history and today's Argentina.


Important info:

Meeting point: Av. Rivadavia and Reconquista (Plaza de Mayo), next to the street sign

We start on time, to make the most of every minute

Wear comfortable shoes

Upon booking, you receive my real-time location and a complimentary PDF guide


\"The best place to understand reality is the street itself.\"

San Telmo is one of the most historic neighborhoods in Buenos Aires: its cobblestones have witnessed much of the city, and its old mansions — abandoned after the yellow fever of 1871 — have turned into tango and art courtyards. I invite you to explore it with me, from the possible founding site to the corner where Mafalda was born. We will walk through Parque Lezama, a green lung and possible cradle of the first Buenos Aires in 1536; the Russian Orthodox Church, with its blue domes that seem like a piece of St. Petersburg; the San Telmo Market and Pasaje Defensa, iron and glass from 1880 among artists and taverns; and Plaza Dorrego and Defensa Street, where tango was born in the courtyards, until we reach the Paseo de la Historieta to meet Mafalda.


And as always, we share some mate along the way to chat about our identity (remember to request it free of charge 2 hours in advance, so I arrive with everything prepared).


Important info:

Meeting point: Monument to Don Pedro de Mendoza (Av. Brasil and Defensa)

We start on time

Bring cash: many artisans at the fair do not accept cards

Upon booking, you receive my real-time location via WhatsApp and a complimentary PDF guide


\"San Telmo is not visited, it is felt.\"

We will walk through the “Historic Center” of the City of Buenos Aires in its center.

We'll observe the historical, sculptural, and architectural icons that distinguish it, such as the Church of San Francisco, the City Museum (Altos de Elorriaga), the Manzana de las Luces (Block of Lights), the San Ignacio Church, the National College of Buenos Aires, the Santo Domingo Complex, Paseo de la Historieta (Historical Walk), Zanjón de Granados (Granados Zane), the Casa Mínima (Minimal House), San Telmo Market, Plaza Dorrego, and the San Pedro Telmo Church. We'll then visit the Puerto Madero neighborhood and visit the iconic Puente de la Mujer (Women's Bridge), where we'll conclude the tour. We'll also remember the historical figures who walked these streets, their lives, and their work.

This historical approach to colonial Buenos Aires and its comparison with the current neighborhood can give us a broader view of the heritage that accompanies it, along with its indisputable visual attractions.

results.name: SAN NICOLÁS: From Plaza Lavalle to Luna Park, the heart that never sleeps
results.description_html:
Have you ever felt the pulse of a city that never sleeps?

San Nicolás is the neighborhood of contrasts: where our flag was born and where today the neon lights of the mythical Corrientes Street shine. Let's discover where the lives of Evita and Perón crossed, what secrets the domes of the Güemes Gallery hold, and why this corner of Buenos Aires was the dream of architects and visionaries. We will walk along Corrientes Avenue, among historic theaters and old bookstores; visit La Ideal Confectionery and the Güemes Gallery, the city's first skyscraper and home to Saint-Exupéry; discover the majesty of the Teatro Colón and the historic Plaza Lavalle; and we will reach, from Luna Park to the Obelisk, the stories that marked the destiny of Belgrano, Perón, and Evita.


If you wish, we will share a free mate experience while we unravel the secrets of the downtown area (request it in advance).


Important information:

Meeting point: Libertad 815 (in front of the Teatro Nacional Cervantes)

We start on time to respect your time and that of the group

Upon booking, I will send you my real-time location via WhatsApp and a complimentary PDF guide of Buenos Aires


"San Nicolás is not visited. It is felt. Between the echo of the Obelisk and the murmur of Corrientes, the city tells you who it was... and who it still is."

results.name: "Recoleta Free Tour: Discover the Elegance and History of Buenos Aires' Aristocratic Legacy"
results.description_html:
Discover the charm of one of the most fascinating neighborhoods in Buenos Aires: Recoleta.

"Although English is not my native language, my passion and enthusiasm for Buenos Aires have inspired me to create this tour in English. With my intermediate-advanced level of English, I hope to offer you an experience that you will truly enjoy." 


On this tour, I will take you to explore its most elegant corners, where history, art, and architecture come together to tell the story of a city that dreamed of becoming a cultural powerhouse in the early 20th century.

You will walk past impressive palaces, European-style mansions, and monuments that witnessed the golden age of Buenos Aires. Throughout the tour, I will reveal the secrets of the most influential families of that time, who left their mark on these majestic buildings.

We will also learn about the work of French landscaper Carlos Thays, who transformed a dry city into a green urban paradise. His vision made Buenos Aires a place full of parks and green spaces, which today bring beauty and life to its historic streets and avenues.

This tour is not just a journey into the past but a unique experience to discover the cultural and architectural evolution of the city.
Get ready to see it with new eyes!!!

results.name: RECOLETA: ARTE, ELEGANCIA Y PODER
results.description_html:
Bienvenidos a Recoleta, el barrio que se viste de gala para que no noten que, debajo del mármol, hay historia, poder, olvido y una Argentina que se niega a mirarse en el espejo.

No venimos a ver mansiones. Venimos a descubrir quiénes las hicieron, quiénes las habitaron y quiénes quedaron afuera.

Este no es un paseo por palacios. Es un recorrido por las decisiones que construyeron (y deshicieron) un país.

¿Sabías que este barrio nació de una epidemia? En 1871, la fiebre amarilla diezmó el sur de la ciudad. Los ricos huyeron. Y eligieron este lugar: más alto, más ventilado, más lejos de los pobres. Así nació Recoleta, no por belleza, sino por exclusión.

Vamos a caminar por la Avenida Alvear, esa calle que parece sacada de París, con mansiones de piedra, balcones de hierro forjado y autos que cuestan más que una casa en el conurbano. Vamos a pararnos frente al Hotel Alvear, el Palacio Duhau, el Jockey Club, el Palacio Pereda, la Nunciatura Apostólica. Y vamos a preguntarnos: ¿Quiénes eran estos hombres que construyeron palacios como si fueran reyes? ¿Qué hicieron con su dinero? ¿Y qué hicieron con su poder?

¿Qué vas a ver?

Plaza de Francia

Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (con entrada)

Plaza Alvear

Iglesia del Pilar

Centro Cultural Recoleta

Cementerio de la Recoleta

Hotel Alvear

Residencia Mc Guire

Palacio Duhau

Palacio de la Nunciatura

Palacio Pereda

Jockey Club

Plaza Carlos Pellegrini

Este tour es para vos si…

No te conformás con decir “qué lindo” y querés saber por qué.

Te interesa la historia, pero no como una lista de fechas, sino como una conversación con el presente.

Querés entender Argentina no desde el asado ni el tango, sino desde sus contradicciones.

Hablás español, sí, pero también quieres escuchar lo que no se dice.

Soy Inés, docente, viajera y cronista. He caminado estos adoquines muchas veces, no como turista, sino como alguien que busca entender. Este tour no es un trabajo. Es una conversación que se renueva cada vez.

 

PUNTO DE ENCUENTRO

Av. del Libertador 1473, en las escalinatas del Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes. 

 

NO LO OLVIDES 

Zapatillas cómodas, agua, ropa ligera.

 

IMPORTANTE: EL PASEO SE SUSPENDE POR LLUVIA

results.name: AVENIDA DE MAYO: From the Cabildo to the Congress, the avenue that wrote history
results.description_html:
From the Casa Rosada to the Congress, there is a route that sums up a large part of Argentine history: the domes and their symbols, the cafes where politics and literature were crafted, the buildings we all pass by but few truly observe. We will walk through Plaza de Mayo —from the Cabildo to the Cathedral where San Martín rests—, discover Dante's mark in the Barolo Palace, and sit with a view of the Tortoni and London City, witnesses of poets and conspiracies, until we reach the dome of the Congress to understand how this path shaped today's Argentina.


And as always, we share some mate along the way (order it free of charge up to 2 hours before the tour) to chat about history and today's Argentina.


Important info:

Meeting point: Av. Rivadavia and Reconquista (Plaza de Mayo), next to the street sign

We start on time, to make the most of every minute

Wear comfortable shoes

Upon booking, you receive my real-time location and a complimentary PDF guide


"The best place to understand reality is the street itself."

results.name: SAN TELMO: From the Cradle of Buenos Aires to the Courtyards of Tango
results.description_html:
San Telmo is one of the most historic neighborhoods in Buenos Aires: its cobblestones have witnessed much of the city, and its old mansions — abandoned after the yellow fever of 1871 — have turned into tango and art courtyards. I invite you to explore it with me, from the possible founding site to the corner where Mafalda was born. We will walk through Parque Lezama, a green lung and possible cradle of the first Buenos Aires in 1536; the Russian Orthodox Church, with its blue domes that seem like a piece of St. Petersburg; the San Telmo Market and Pasaje Defensa, iron and glass from 1880 among artists and taverns; and Plaza Dorrego and Defensa Street, where tango was born in the courtyards, until we reach the Paseo de la Historieta to meet Mafalda.


And as always, we share some mate along the way to chat about our identity (remember to request it free of charge 2 hours in advance, so I arrive with everything prepared).


Important info:

Meeting point: Monument to Don Pedro de Mendoza (Av. Brasil and Defensa)

We start on time

Bring cash: many artisans at the fair do not accept cards

Upon booking, you receive my real-time location via WhatsApp and a complimentary PDF guide


"San Telmo is not visited, it is felt."

results.name: Historic Center. Where our identity was born.
results.description_html:
We will walk through the “Historic Center” of the City of Buenos Aires in its center.

We'll observe the historical, sculptural, and architectural icons that distinguish it, such as the Church of San Francisco, the City Museum (Altos de Elorriaga), the Manzana de las Luces (Block of Lights), the San Ignacio Church, the National College of Buenos Aires, the Santo Domingo Complex, Paseo de la Historieta (Historical Walk), Zanjón de Granados (Granados Zane), the Casa Mínima (Minimal House), San Telmo Market, Plaza Dorrego, and the San Pedro Telmo Church. We'll then visit the Puerto Madero neighborhood and visit the iconic Puente de la Mujer (Women's Bridge), where we'll conclude the tour. We'll also remember the historical figures who walked these streets, their lives, and their work.

This historical approach to colonial Buenos Aires and its comparison with the current neighborhood can give us a broader view of the heritage that accompanies it, along with its indisputable visual attractions.
